ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
As shown in the circuit in Figure 1, the number of turns of the solenoid coil is $n=2000$, the cross-sectional area of the solenoid is $S=40\mathrm{cm}^{2}$, the total resistance of the coil is $r=1\Omega$, the fixed resistors are $R_{1}=2\Omega$ and $R_{2}=5\Omega$, and the parallel-plate capacitor has its plates P and Q placed horizontally with a distance $d=10\mathrm{cm}$ between them. The magnetic induction intensity $B$ of the uniform magnetic field passing through the solenoid varies with time $t$ as shown in Figure 2. After closing switch S and allowing the circuit to stabilize, a charged particle located between the two plates of the capacitor is found to be in a stationary state. The gravitational acceleration is known to be $g=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$.

1. What is the electrical power consumed by the resistor $R_{1}$?
2. What is the specific charge of a charged particle?

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in the circuit in Figure 1, the number of turns of the solenoid coil is $n=2000$, the cross-sectional area of the solenoid is $S=40\mathrm{cm}^{2}$, the total resistance of the coil is $r=1\Omega$, the fixed resistors are $R_{1}=2\Omega$ and $R_{2}=5\Omega$, and the parallel-plate capacitor has its plates P and Q placed horizontally with a distance $d=10\mathrm{cm}$ between them. The magnetic induction intensity $B$ of the uniform magnetic field passing through the solenoid varies with time $t$ as shown in Figure 2. After closing switch S and allowing the circuit to stabilize, a charged particle located between the two plates of the capacitor is found to be in a stationary state. The gravitational acceleration is known to be $g=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$. 1. What is the electrical power consumed by the resistor $R_{1}$? 2. What is the specific charge of a charged particle?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: On the left side in Figure 1 is a solenoid in magnetic field B, and the solenoid is connected to an external circuit; above it, resistor R1 is connected in series, and on the right side there is resistor R2. The two plates of capacitor C are placed horizontally, the upper plate is labeled P, the lower plate is labeled Q, and the capacitor and R2 are connected between the same upper and lower two nodes, so the capacitor and R2 are in parallel. Below there is switch S. Figure 2 is a B-t graph, and the magnetic flux density decreases linearly from 0.6 T at t=0 to 0.2 T at t=0.2 s. Reasoning: First convert units, S=40 cm^2=4.0×10^-3 m^2, d=10 cm=0.10 m. From the linear-change section of Figure 2, the magnitude of the rate of change of magnetic flux density is |dB/dt|=(0.6-0.2)/0.2=2 T/s. The magnitude of the induced electromotive force produced by the solenoid is ε=nS|dB/dt|=2000×4.0×10^-3×2=16 V. After the circuit becomes stable, the capacitor branch is equivalent to an open circuit, and the current only passes through the coil resistance r, R1, and R2, so the total resistance Rtotal=r+R1+R2=1+2+5=8 Ω, and the current I=ε/Rtotal=16/8=2 A. The electric power consumed by R1 is P_R1=I^2R1=2^2×2=8 W. The capacitor and R2 are in parallel, so the voltage across the capacitor is equal to the voltage across R2: U_C=IR2=2×5=10 V. The magnitude of the electric field strength between the two plates is E=U_C/d=10/0.10=100 V/m. The charged particle is stationary, and the forces are balanced; the magnitude of the electric force is equal to the magnitude of gravity, namely qE=mg, so the magnitude of the charge-to-mass ratio is q/m=g/E=10/100=0.1 C/kg.
